articles.body: Transactions & activity View the active wallet’s full transaction history Review available coin and token activity together across the active wallet’s networks. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Bottom navigation → History How to do it Tap the history icon, shown as a clock with a circular arrow, in the bottom navigation. Review the most recent available entries, grouped by date. Each row identifies the action and asset, its time, and available amounts. Scroll for older entries and use the additional-activity control when it is shown to load more saved history. Tap an entry to open its transaction details, or use the filter icon in the top bar to narrow the list. To look for a particular transaction, select History and then the separate Search icon. Return to Wallet when you want the portfolio view. This view combines available activity for the active wallet. It does not merge unrelated wallets, and Solana activity follows the currently selected Solana address path. A history row represents an asset’s activity within a transaction. One blockchain transaction can therefore produce more than one row when multiple assets are involved. “Full history” means the available records for this wallet, after safety filtering. Provider limits, incomplete synchronization and unsupported historical details can leave gaps. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 History shows activity for the selected wallet. Open a row for its status, network, identifiers and fee; these rows are illustrative. See step 1 . 2 Read the amount and status separately. The ellipsis at the top contains screenshot sharing, link sharing and the explorer action. Good to know If an expected entry is absent, clear search and filters, refresh Home or the asset, and compare the exact public account on its network explorer.

articles.title: Search transactions by ID, address or amount
articles.summary: Find a transaction using information you already know, within the active wallet’s available history.
articles.body: Transactions & activity Search transactions by ID, address or amount Find a transaction using information you already know, within the active wallet’s available history. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Bottom navigation → History → Search How to do it Tap History first, then the separate magnifying-glass Search icon. Confirm the field says Search transactions. Enter a transaction ID, sender or recipient address, asset name, symbol, or network. You can also search an amount in native units or an available displayed local-currency amount. Add a currency code or symbol when it helps distinguish a fiat value. Open a result to compare its full transaction ID, network, addresses and status. If a result is missing, clear the query and any active filters, then try the exact transaction ID or address. To search assets again, select Wallet before Search. Search works across available stored history before the visible page limit. An address can match supplied sender or recipient information even if the list shows only one representative counterparty. Amount searches use available prices and the selected display currency. A local-currency match may change with the quote; a transaction ID is a more stable way to identify a transfer. History filters remain in effect during history search. Searching does not bypass spam filtering or fetch records a provider has never supplied. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 History search is scoped to transactions. Clear the query or filters when a known entry is not visible. See step 1 . 2 History shows activity for the selected wallet. Open a row for its status, network, identifiers and fee; these rows are illustrative. Good to know A short address fragment or common amount can match several entries. Compare the complete transaction ID before treating a result as the transfer you intended.

articles.title: Filter transaction history
articles.summary: Narrow activity by network, asset, direction, status, date and quantity without changing the underlying records.
articles.body: Transactions & activity Filter transaction history Narrow activity by network, asset, direction, status, date and quantity without changing the underlying records. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it History → filter icon How to do it Open History and tap the filter icon in the top bar. The sheet starts with your current selections. Choose one or more Networks and Assets when those choices are available. Asset choices refer to an exact asset on its network, not just a shared ticker. Choose transaction types such as Sent, Received or self-transfers, and any statuses you want to include. Select a date period or custom start and end dates. Optionally enter a minimum, maximum or both under Amount. Tap the native checkmark to apply the choices. Cancel or dismiss the sheet to leave the current results unchanged. Use the active filter chips above the results to remove individual categories, or choose Reset Filters to clear them. If resetting inside the sheet, tap the checkmark to apply that reset. Selections within one category are alternatives; categories combine. For example, Received plus USDC plus a date range means incoming USDC entries in that range. Amount limits are measured in the asset’s native units, not local currency. A minimum of 10 means 10 tokens or coins. Select one asset first when you need a meaningful quantity comparison. Today uses the current calendar day. The seven-day and thirty-day periods include today; custom dates include both selected days. Entries without a usable timestamp may not match a date filter. The number on the filter button counts active filter categories, not individual selected networks or assets. In one asset’s View All screen, the asset and account scope is fixed, so broader network and asset selectors are omitted. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Choose the desired transaction filters and review the resulting scope. Filtering hides rows; it does not remove on-chain transactions. See step 1 . 2 History shows activity for the selected wallet. Open a row for its status, network, identifiers and fee; these rows are illustrative. Good to know A disabled checkmark means a range needs correction, such as a minimum above its maximum or a start date after its end. No matching results can simply mean the combined filters are too narrow.

articles.title: View all transactions for one coin or token
articles.summary: Move from an asset’s five-entry preview to a dedicated history for that exact asset and account.
articles.body: Transactions & activity View all transactions for one coin or token Move from an asset’s five-entry preview to a dedicated history for that exact asset and account. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Wallet → asset → Activity → View All How to do it Open the coin or token from Wallet or Search and scroll to Activity. The preview shows up to five latest visible entries. Each row names the action and asset and shows its time and available amounts. When more than five visible entries are available, tap View All at the end of the preview. Browse older entries on the new screen. Search there or use its filter icon to narrow the same asset’s history. Tap a transaction for details, or go back to the asset screen. Use the bottom History view separately for activity across the wallet. View All stays limited to the selected token or coin, its account and its network. Opening USDT on one network does not include another network’s USDT or every token on that chain. If there are five or fewer visible entries, there is no View All button because the preview already contains all currently available entries. The threshold is based on visible history after safety filtering. Hidden spam and unavailable provider records do not force the button to appear. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 The asset page separates the owned quantity, market price/chart and account activity. This example uses synthetic market values. See step 1 . 2 Read the amount and status separately. The ellipsis at the top contains screenshot sharing, link sharing and the explorer action. Good to know An absent View All button is not proof that no other on-chain activity ever occurred. Check the correct account and explorer if a known transaction is missing.

articles.title: How Oath hides spam and phishing activity
articles.summary: Understand why suspicious or unverified token entries can be absent from your activity lists.
articles.body: Security & privacy How Oath hides spam and phishing activity Understand why suspicious or unverified token entries can be absent from your activity lists. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it History, asset Activity and transaction search How to do it Use History or an asset’s Activity as usual. Safety filtering runs automatically; no separate switch is required. If an unexpected token is absent, check whether it is unverified or has a suspicious name containing a link or a claim instruction. For an expected legitimate transfer, verify the network, public account and full token contract or asset identity using independent information. For supported manual-lookup networks, you can deliberately add a token you recognize through Wallet → Search. Review the full identity before adding it. If a discrepancy remains, compare the public explorer record or contact support with the network and transaction ID. The same visibility rules apply to the full history, asset previews, transaction search, filter choices and transaction details. Previously saved activity is also checked, so old spam does not need a fresh arrival to be hidden. Oath combines available provider verification with network-specific asset catalogs and local checks. A token is matched by its network and exact contract, mint, issuer or asset reference. Matching a popular symbol or having a quoted price is not enough. Unlisted tokens are hidden by default from history unless you have explicitly chosen to track them. Explicit tracking does not override detected phishing metadata, known blocked-token evidence or zero-value transfer rules. Filtering changes the app’s presentation. It does not delete public blockchain records, reverse a transfer or revoke a contract allowance. The explorer can still show entries that Oath hides. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 History shows activity for the selected wallet. Open a row for its status, network, identifiers and fee; these rows are illustrative. See step 1 . 2 Read the amount and status separately. The ellipsis at the top contains screenshot sharing, link sharing and the explorer action. Good to know No filter can recognize every scam, and an unlisted token is not automatically fraudulent. Never follow a claim link from unsolicited token metadata or use a lookalike address copied from unfamiliar activity.

articles.title: Why can a transaction show zero?
articles.summary: Distinguish a rounded fiat amount, a zero-value contract action and a hidden spam transfer.
articles.body: Transactions & activity Why can a transaction show zero? Distinguish a rounded fiat amount, a zero-value contract action and a hidden spam transfer. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it History → transaction details How to do it Compare the local-currency amount with the native quantity underneath it. If the local value rounds to zero but the native quantity is nonzero, the transfer can simply be too small to display at that currency’s normal precision. If the native amount is also zero, open the transaction and check its status, network fee and explorer record. For an outgoing native-coin entry, consider whether it records a contract call or another action that transfers no native coin but still has a network fee. If you do not recognize the activity, compare the complete sender, recipient and transaction ID. Do not rely on a short address fragment. Zero-value incoming transfers and ordinary zero-value token-transfer entries are hidden by the history safety rules. Attackers can use such entries to put lookalike addresses into a wallet’s activity. Oath can retain zero-value outgoing or self native-coin actions, and zero-value outgoing outcomes such as Failed, Canceled or Replaced. Hiding every zero would also hide meaningful actions. A zero local-currency display, an unavailable quote and a zero native transfer are different situations. The detailed public transaction helps distinguish them. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 History shows activity for the selected wallet. Open a row for its status, network, identifiers and fee; these rows are illustrative. See step 1 . 2 Read the amount and status separately. The ellipsis at the top contains screenshot sharing, link sharing and the explorer action. Good to know Filtering a zero-value entry is not the same as canceling it. On-chain records and any fees already paid are separate from the app’s activity display.

articles.title: Understand verified and manually added tokens
articles.summary: Learn why automatic discovery can omit a token and what changes when you choose to track it.
articles.body: Assets & networks Understand verified and manually added tokens Learn why automatic discovery can omit a token and what changes when you choose to track it. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Wallet → Assets, or Wallet → Search → token address How to do it First confirm the active wallet and the network on which you expect the token. If the token is absent, check its full contract, mint or asset reference using information you trust independently. For supported EVM networks, TRON or Solana, select Wallet then Search and paste the exact token address. Review every matching result’s network and token identity. Add only the intended token, then finish with the checkmark. Return to the asset and review any available quantity, quote and activity. Refresh if a recent transfer has not appeared. Automatic token discovery uses available verification lists. A new or obscure legitimate token can be missing from a list, so “unverified” does not by itself mean “scam.” Manually adding a supported token records your choice to track it. It does not verify its issuer, grant spending permission, buy the token, or guarantee a price and complete history. History still hides identified phishing metadata, blocked tokens and protected zero-value transfers even when a token is tracked. An explorer may therefore show more raw activity than Oath. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Use Wallet search for an asset name or exact supported token identity. A token symbol alone does not establish its network. See step 1 . 2 Review the network, full contract reference, name and symbol before adding a token. A logo is not a security guarantee. Good to know Never decide by symbol alone. Tokens with the same name on the same or different networks can have different contracts and issuers.

articles.title: Use the checkmark to finish an action
articles.summary: The native checkmark replaces text Done controls in supported screens and sheets.
articles.body: Settings & support Use the checkmark to finish an action The native checkmark replaces text Done controls in supported screens and sheets. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Wallet editing, token completion and history filters How to do it When you have finished reordering wallets, tap the checkmark in the top bar instead of looking for a text Done button. After Add Token succeeds, use the checkmark confirmation to finish that sheet. In history filters, choose your options and tap the checkmark to apply the complete selection. If the confirmation is disabled, finish the operation or correct any invalid field before trying again. With VoiceOver, listen for the action name, such as Done or Apply. The visual icon still has a localized accessibility label. The checkmark is an action control, and its meaning follows the screen you are on. It can finish editing, close a completed flow or apply a draft. Cancel, Close, Back and destructive actions keep their own purposes. Do not use the checkmark as a substitute for reading a removal or permanent-deletion confirmation. Native alerts, keyboards and browser controls are drawn by iOS and can use system-provided labels. Older supported iOS versions can also display a different native treatment. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Choose the desired transaction filters and review the resulting scope. Filtering hides rows; it does not remove on-chain transactions. See step 1 . 2 Names, colors, balances and the active badge distinguish wallets. Choose the intended wallet before starting an action. Good to know The small check badge on a wallet icon means that wallet is active. It is different from the tappable checkmark used to finish an action.

articles.title: Authenticate before opening Passcode & Face ID
articles.summary: Protect changes to app security with a separate authentication step.
articles.body: Security & privacy Authenticate before opening Passcode & Face ID Protect changes to app security with a separate authentication step. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Settings → Passcode & Face ID How to do it Open the main Settings screen from the sliders icon at the top of Home. Tap Passcode & Face ID. If biometric protection is enabled, complete the biometric prompt. If biometrics are disabled or the flow offers a passcode fallback, enter your current app passcode. After authentication, review or change passcode protection, biometrics, Require Passcode timing or App Switcher Privacy. If you cancel authentication, return to Settings and start again when ready. Unlocking the app and entering its security settings are separate checks. Returning after the app locks can require authentication again. If app passcode protection is disabled, there is no existing app passcode to enter. You can access the screen to set one, then confirm the new six-digit code. When you finish enabling a new passcode, Oath attempts biometric setup when available. Turning on Face ID itself uses the biometric prompt rather than another current-passcode entry inside that enable flow. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Enter the existing app passcode to unlock. No digits or biometric credentials are shown in this example. See step 1 . 2 Security settings group passcode, biometric, locking and app-switcher privacy controls. No authentication secret is shown. Good to know Your app passcode is not your recovery phrase, BIP-39 passphrase or iCloud backup password. Security changes do not replace a separate recovery backup.

articles.title: Open and search the Help Center
articles.summary: Find a feature’s instructions inside Oath and return to the app when you are finished.
articles.body: Settings & support Open and search the Help Center Find a feature’s instructions inside Oath and return to the app when you are finished. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Settings → Help Center How to do it Return to the top of Home and tap the sliders icon to open Settings. Tap Help Center to open help.oathwallet.org in the native in-app browser. Search a feature or question, or choose a collection such as Your wallets or Transactions & activity. Open a guide and follow its Where to find it route and numbered steps. Use Related articles for connected features. Close the in-app browser to return to Oath. Use Contact Us, Submit a Bug or Request a Feature from Settings if you need a different kind of help. Each guide describes one feature or question and identifies the app version it covers. Older release articles at articles.oathwallet.org can describe a different interface. The Help Center is readable without importing a wallet or providing recovery material. Article screenshots use example wallets; do not send funds to example addresses. Submit a Bug and Request a Feature open the project’s issue page. Contact Us opens an email draft to care@oathwallet.org; writing a draft does not send it automatically. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Open the appropriate settings row for wallets, backup, security, contacts, appearance or support. See step 1 . 2 About provides the Articles, Privacy Policy and Terms of Service links. These open external content; review the destination before interacting. Good to know Never put a recovery phrase, private key, app passcode or backup password into a support form or message. Public transaction IDs are normally enough to start a transaction investigation.

articles.title: Use Max and understand spendable balance
articles.summary: See why the maximum you can send may be lower than the total displayed on Home.
articles.body: Send & receive Use Max and understand spendable balance See why the maximum you can send may be lower than the total displayed on Home. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Send → amount → Max → review How to do it Select the intended asset and enter the recipient first. Tap Max on the amount page. Read the resulting quantity in asset units. For token transfers, check that you also hold the network’s native fee asset. Continue to review and read the network fee plus any activation, reserve or storage requirement. If the available amount changes, return to amount and calculate Max again. Confirm only after reviewing the updated total. Check History after submission; do not repeatedly send because a balance refresh is delayed. Native-coin Max needs to leave enough for transaction costs. UTXO fees depend on inputs and transaction size; account-based networks may retain mandatory balances or reserves. For a token, the entire token balance may be transferable while a different native asset pays gas. A token with no reliable quote can still be entered in asset units. Fee estimates are network-specific and can change. A maximum fee is a spending limit or estimate used in that review, not a promise that the exact amount will be charged. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Enter the asset amount, inspect the available balance and use Max or the local-currency switch only when appropriate. See step 1 . 2 Use the exact required network and native fee asset. The example guidance is not a request to fund a help-center address. Good to know A displayed portfolio total is a valuation, not a promise that all of it is spendable.

articles.title: Enter destination tags and memos
articles.summary: Include the extra reference an exchange or shared receiving account needs to credit your transfer.
articles.body: Send & receive Enter destination tags and memos Include the extra reference an exchange or shared receiving account needs to credit your transfer. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Send → recipient → memo or destination tag How to do it Open the recipient’s deposit instructions and confirm the asset and network. In Oath, select that asset and paste the deposit address. For XRP Ledger enter the requested destination tag. For Stellar select the required memo type before entering its exact value. For other networks with a memo field, follow the recipient’s instructions exactly; do not invent a memo if none is required. Review the address, memo/tag, amount and network together on the final screen. After sending, retain the transaction ID. If an exchange does not credit it, contact that exchange with the public transaction details. An exchange may use one address for many customers and distinguish deposits with a tag or memo. A valid address alone can therefore be insufficient. Text memos, numeric IDs and hashes are different formats. Use the field and type displayed for the selected chain; leading characters and case can matter. Oath cannot assign a missing deposit to your exchange account after broadcast. Do not resend a second payment merely to fix a tag on the first. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Paste, scan or select a public recipient, then verify its complete address and the network before continuing. See step 1 . Good to know Memos and on-chain messages can become public. Never put a recovery phrase, private key, password or personal secret in them.

articles.title: Set Bitcoin transfer options
articles.summary: Understand Replace by fee and the optional public on-chain message before sending.
articles.body: Send & receive Set Bitcoin transfer options Understand Replace by fee and the optional public on-chain message before sending. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Bitcoin → Send → amount → transfer options How to do it Choose Bitcoin, enter the recipient and continue to the amount page. Open Transfer options from the amount page. Enable Replace by fee only if you want the transaction to signal replacement eligibility. The option is off by default. Optionally enter an on-chain message. Read the byte count and network-specific limit. Confirm the options with the checkmark, then review the updated transaction and fee. After broadcast, use the transaction’s status and explorer to follow it. Enabling RBF does not itself submit a replacement. The message is stored publicly with the transfer using OP_RETURN and contributes to transaction size and fees. A byte count is not necessarily the same as a character count. Bitcoin node policies differ. Larger messages can be rejected by stricter nodes even when they fit the app’s supported limit. RBF signals replacement policy; some Bitcoin nodes allow replacement even when that signal is off. The switch is not a guarantee that an unconfirmed transaction cannot be replaced. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Review Replace by fee and the optional public on-chain message. A message is public and adds transaction data and possible fees. See step 1 . 2 Enter the asset amount, inspect the available balance and use Max or the local-currency switch only when appropriate. Good to know Never put secrets in an on-chain message. Confirmed blockchain content cannot be edited like a chat message.

articles.title: Resolve a transfer that cannot be sent
articles.summary: Work out whether the problem is validation, fees, authorization, provider access or an uncertain submission.
articles.body: Send & receive Resolve a transfer that cannot be sent Work out whether the problem is validation, fees, authorization, provider access or an uncertain submission. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Send → review or result How to do it Read the error and identify whether it occurred before authorization, during submission or while waiting for confirmation. Check the selected wallet, recipient network, token identity and any required memo or tag. Check the native fee balance and account activation, reserve or registration guidance. Reduce the amount if needed. If authentication was canceled, return to the review and authenticate again. Never enter your recovery phrase into a dApp or support form. If Oath has a transaction ID or reports a pending/uncertain submission, inspect that same transaction in History or its explorer before attempting another transfer. If it is definitely failed or rejected, correct the reason and make a fresh review. Contact support with the network, public transaction ID and error text if needed. A local validation error normally means a transfer has not been prepared. A lost response after broadcast is different: the network may already have the transaction. Simulation and preflight failures can reflect insufficient funds, slippage, a changed allowance or contract conditions. Repeatedly confirming unchanged data does not fix those conditions. Keep Oath available for status checks. Background work can pause when iOS suspends the app; reopening and unlocking lets pending work resume. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 A failed check needs investigation. Recheck the route, amount, fees and dApp request instead of assuming it is safe to retry. See step 1 . 2 Pending is not confirmed. Check the same transaction identifier before submitting another request. Good to know Do not send recovery words, private keys, passcodes or raw signing payloads to support.

articles.title: Connect a dApp with WalletConnect
articles.summary: Approve the intended website, wallet and networks before responding to a dApp request.
articles.body: dApps & permissions Connect a dApp with WalletConnect Approve the intended website, wallet and networks before responding to a dApp request. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it dApp → Connect wallet → WalletConnect → Oath How to do it Open the dApp from a trusted address and choose WalletConnect in its wallet connection options. On another screen, scan its WalletConnect QR using Oath’s Home scanner. On the same device, choose the Oath link offered by the dApp. Unlock Oath if asked. Read the connection proposal’s website identity and any verification warning. Choose the intended wallet and approve only the networks you need. Review the methods being requested. Connect, then return to the dApp. A connection shares the approved public accounts; it does not approve every future signature or transfer. Review each later request independently. Manage the connection in Settings → WalletConnect or Permissions → Connected DApps. WalletConnect support depends on the namespace and request method. Oath supports EVM, THORChain and Solana request flows within their implemented limits; it does not imply every network in the portfolio supports every dApp. A familiar name or icon can be copied. Compare the website origin and reject unexpected, blocked or unverified requests when you cannot establish why they appeared. Pairing requests expire. If the proposal is no longer usable, start a fresh connection from the dApp instead of reusing an old QR. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Inspect the site identity, wallet, requested networks and access before connecting. This proposal is an offline fixture. See step 1 . 2 Read verification warnings and decline a request if you cannot establish the site’s identity and purpose. Good to know Never share a WalletConnect pairing QR or URI publicly. Connecting does not require giving a site your recovery phrase or private key.

articles.title: Disconnect a dApp safely
articles.summary: End a WalletConnect session and separately review any on-chain permissions you granted.
articles.body: dApps & permissions Disconnect a dApp safely End a WalletConnect session and separately review any on-chain permissions you granted. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it Settings → WalletConnect, or Permissions → Connected DApps How to do it Open the connected-apps list and choose the wallet whose sessions you want to inspect. Identify the session by its website and approved accounts/networks. Open its controls and disconnect the intended session. Return to the list and verify that it is no longer connected. Reconnect from the dApp if you later need it. Open Permissions → Token access or Collectible access if you also want to revoke previously granted allowances. Review and confirm those revocations separately, then check their results. A WalletConnect session allows a dApp to request actions. Disconnecting removes that session’s access to this wallet connection. Disconnecting does not revoke on-chain allowances. A previously signed permit may also remain usable until its expiry or an applicable invalidation. Disconnecting is not an on-chain transaction and does not reverse a completed swap or transfer. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Open a connection to inspect approved access or disconnect it. This is an offline demo session, not a live connected site. See step 1 . 2 A connection confirmation concerns approved public accounts. Each later signature or transfer needs its own review. Good to know If a site still displays an old connected state, refresh it. Check Oath’s session list and on-chain permission status separately.

articles.title: Review a token swap from a dApp
articles.summary: Understand which asset you pay, which asset you expect, and the network and limits you are authorizing.
articles.body: dApps & permissions Review a token swap from a dApp Understand which asset you pay, which asset you expect, and the network and limits you are authorizing. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it dApp → Swap → Oath approval How to do it Choose the input asset, output asset, amount and network in the dApp. Request its quote. When Oath opens, confirm the dApp origin, selected wallet/account and network. Read the input and output assets using their full identities. Check whether an amount is exact, a maximum input or a minimum output. Review the recipient, native-coin value, network fee and deadline when shown. A token approval or Permit2 signature may arrive as a separate request before the swap. Open Transaction data for readable operations and the original technical data. If an unfamiliar call cannot be explained, reject it until you can verify its purpose. Confirm and authenticate only the request you intended. Return to the dApp for any remaining step, then verify the actual transaction outcome. For recognized router methods Oath displays readable swap bounds and routing operations. Native wrapping/unwrapping is only summarized when the route supports that interpretation. A quote or simulation is not a guaranteed settlement price. Slippage, price movement, expiry and contract conditions can cause a swap to fail. Unknown routers, commands or metadata remain explicitly unknown or technical. A safe review must not invent an output token or interpret every arbitrary contract call as a swap. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. No live funds were sent, swapped or revoked for these examples. Never send funds to an example address. Tap an image to inspect it at full size. 1 Review the source token, amount, destination token and minimum output in this decoded unsigned swap example. See step 1 . 2 Review the spender and allowance limit. This unsigned example does not grant permission on-chain. 3 When an action cannot be fully decoded, inspect the contract and original data. Do not assume an unknown request is a harmless transfer. Good to know An approval grants spending access; it is not the swap itself. Verify the spender and limit, then review the separate swap request.

articles.title: Read human-readable transaction data
articles.summary: Use the decoded details to understand a contract request while keeping the exact technical payload available.
articles.body: dApps & permissions Read human-readable transaction data Use the decoded details to understand a contract request while keeping the exact technical payload available. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it dApp approval → Transaction data How to do it On a transaction approval, check the network, account, destination contract and native value first. Open Transaction data. Read the recognized method and its fields: for example recipient, asset, spending limit, swap path or deadline. Do not approve simply because a method name looks familiar. Return to the review and confirm only after the decoded operation agrees with your intended action. Decoding describes the submitted instructions; it does not certify a contract as safe or show every possible effect of its execution. Token decimals are resolved for the exact asset. When reliable metadata is missing, exact raw units or addresses are safer than an invented name or amount. Some complex or unsupported contracts cannot be completely decoded. Reject or independently verify those requests rather than assuming a generic label means a harmless transfer. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. articles.title: Review messages, sign-ins and token permits
articles.summary: Tell a login challenge apart from a message, token approval or spending authorization.
articles.body: dApps & permissions Review messages, sign-ins and token permits Tell a login challenge apart from a message, token approval or spending authorization. Oath 4.0.3 Where to find it WalletConnect request → review How to do it Check which website requested the signature and why you expect it now. Read the full message or structured fields. For sign-in, compare the domain, address and any expiry or nonce details. For an approval or permit, inspect the token, spender, amount/limit, chain and deadline rather than treating it as a login. If an editable approval limit is offered, choose only the allowance you intend and review the resulting request. Reject unreadable, unexpected or unsupported requests. Authenticate only when the requested authorization makes sense. After signing, return to the dApp. Manage any resulting on-chain allowance in Permissions. A message signature may have no immediate network fee but can still authorize an action. Permit signatures can grant spending rights when submitted later. Signing a transaction and broadcasting it are distinct. A dApp can ask for signed bytes and submit them itself; the absence of an immediate History entry does not mean the signature is harmless. A signature cannot generally be recalled by disconnecting the session. Available nonce invalidation and revocation mechanisms depend on the exact permission. Follow the pending result without resubmitting the same removal unnecessarily. Open Recent changes and refresh the permission scan. Treat access as removed only after its result is verified. Removal uses the permission type’s supported instruction: for example an EVM/TRON allowance reset or a Solana token-account delegate revocation. A transaction can confirm yet fail to remove the expected access if state changed or the contract behaves differently. Oath checks the resulting permission rather than relying only on a transaction hash. An NFT collection approval, token allowance, account-control delegation and permanent token delegate have different scopes. Not every row can be revoked by the current account. You may continue using the app while the queue processes supported items; one failed item does not prevent later items from being attempted. Open Recent changes. Check confirmed, pending and failed results individually, then correct failures and retry only the outstanding items. Each network can require its own transaction and fee. A batch is not a single atomic transaction and may finish with mixed results. The queue can continue while the app is usable, but iOS can suspend background execution. Reopen and unlock Oath to resume when required; do not assume it runs indefinitely after closing the app. Refresh coverage after completion. Verify the updated state after confirmation. If the permission is permanent, unsupported or cannot be safely changed by this account, do not assume a token-level revoke will remove it. A Token-2022 permanent delegate is part of the mint’s authority design; an individual holder cannot simply revoke that authority like an ordinary token-account delegate. A familiar asset logo or a small current balance does not make broad account control harmless. Read the scope before acting. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. If Recently Deleted contains wallets, review the first prompt and agree to include those wallets in permanent removal only if you have their required recovery material. Read the final reset confirmation. Both confirmations must be accepted before deletion starts; cancel here if you need to preserve any wallet. Confirm the final removal and wait for the local reset to finish. Do not interpret the first confirmation alone as completed deletion. Oath returns to Welcome. To use a wallet again, import its recovery material or restore an encrypted backup. The final wallet is not left as the only item in Recently Deleted. The flow clears retained wallets before resetting the installation to its no-wallet state. This removes local access and app data. Blockchain funds and previously granted on-chain permissions are unaffected; deleting a wallet does not revoke access. Existing cloud backup files are separate. Keep the correct password and any extra recovery passphrase needed to restore them. Follow along in Oath Real app screens with illustrative demo data. See step 1 . 2 Read the deletion deadline. Open Oath and enter your existing app passcode if requested. Let the loading/unlock flow finish. On Home, check the selected wallet and open Wallets to review the names of your other wallets. Compare receiving addresses on the intended networks before transferring. Balances and history may take time to refresh. If the upgrade cannot safely import a wallet type, stop and follow the error guidance rather than resetting or creating a replacement wallet over it. The upgrade preserves compatible wallet material and names using the new wallet rules. Unsupported multisig or multi-key collections are stopped safely rather than silently reduced to a different wallet. An existing passcode is preserved where compatible. Biometric authorization can require a fresh system prompt; it must not be assumed from an old toggle alone. Cached blockchain information is disposable and fetched again.
